% ============================================================
\section{Introduction}
% ============================================================

% --- Research question -------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Research question}

This thesis asks a single question: \textbf{do cities with student synthetic
biology research also produce academic papers in related areas?} Put more
carefully: when a city's iGEM teams take up a theme, do that city's researchers
publish on related themes, and can we see the relatedness in the text both groups
leave behind? The chapters that follow build the data and the measures to answer
it, then test that answer to breaking point. Throughout, we speak of
\textit{semantic relatedness} and \textit{co-location}, and we avoid the language
of cause and effect.

\subsection{Synthetic Biology}

Humanity has always sought to understand and influence the natural world. Biology,
the study of life itself, spent most of its history describing it, breaking
organisms into their parts to work out the principles that hold them together.
That descriptive work gave rise to something new. Once we understood life's
principles well enough, we began to \textit{write} with them, designing and
directing new biological systems of our own. This is the age of Synthetic Biology:
a field that treats genetic sequences as functions in the programming language of
life, standardises them, and snaps them together into genetic circuits
\citep{wayIntegratingBiologicalRedesign2014}. A living cell becomes a kind of
programmable factory. A single sequence might switch a gene on, report a signal,
or drive a metabolic pathway. The parts compose much like software, and the living
machinery that results is a tool we can aim at problems of our own choosing.

That shift from describing life to engineering it is recent, and it is moving
fast. In a couple of decades Synthetic Biology has grown from a handful of
proof-of-concept circuits into a field with real stakes in medicine, materials,
agriculture, and energy
\citep{shapiraTrackingEmergenceSynthetic2017, raimbaultMappingEmergenceSynthetic2016}.
It is also hard to pin down. Its boundaries keep moving, and its vocabulary
overlaps heavily with the descriptive molecular biology it grew out of. A young
field this consequential is worth watching closely, and worth asking where its
innovation happens and who is doing it.

\subsection{iGEM}

One arena where that innovation takes shape early is iGEM. The International
Genetically Engineered Machine competition is a worldwide student contest in
Synthetic Biology, a sort of LEGO-robotics contest for genetic engineering. Teams
of students, usually hosted by a university, spend most of a year designing and
building an original project with the tools of the field. Every team starts from
the same kit of standardised parts and the same basic rules, then is left to
invent its own entry. They document that entry in public on a project ``wiki'', a
page that reads much like an extended research abstract
\citep{santoliniIGEMModelSystem2023}.

iGEM matters here for more than its scale. For many researchers it is a first
serious project in Synthetic Biology, and a launching point for a career in
academia or industry. Its alumni have founded companies and started labs of their
own. iGEM styles itself as ``the heart of synthetic biology,'' and it isn't only
hype. The competition also sets norms that reach well beyond it: open science,
thorough public documentation, and a shared registry of standardised,
interoperable parts. Those norms are what make iGEM legible to a study like this
one. Thousands of projects, each documented the same way and each tied to a place
and a year, add up to a detailed record of a field as it grows.

% --- Argument and central claim ---------------------------------------------
\subsection{From iGEM to a testable claim}

That record is what makes iGEM worth studying, because it sits near the base of a
larger chain. Innovation rests on research: new products grow out of people
investigating what is possible. Synthetic Biology is one of the most active
frontiers of that work, and iGEM is where a large share of its practitioners first
learn to do it. If we want to know how innovation in the field takes root, and how
its ideas travel, the student projects at the entry point are a natural place to
start.

This thesis makes one central, testable claim. When a city's student teams take up
a theme, say biosensors or carbon capture, that city's published papers should
concentrate in related areas, more than they would in a city that produced the
same amount of work on unrelated themes. The claim is about \textit{relatedness}:
whether student and academic work sit in the same corners of the field in the same
places. It is not a claim about cause. Everything that follows is built to state
it precisely, then try hard to knock it down.

% --- The artifacts -----------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Reading capabilities off artifacts}

Capabilities are abstract, so we read them off the concrete things a place
produces. Each kind of artifact records the creation of new knowledge in its own
way, while pointing back to the same underlying capability. An academic paper is
the currency of scholarship, rewarded by its influence on a field. A patent is a
claim on commercial value, filed because someone expects an idea to pay. The two
often diverge. A landmark result can have no obvious market, and a lucrative
patent can hold little that is scientifically new. Synthetic Biology adds a third
kind of record that few fields keep so openly: the student project, published in
full by teams still learning the craft. Different as these artifacts are in
audience and incentive, they grow out of the same local pool of people and
equipment, which is why comparing them can tell us something about a place.

This thesis works with four such artifacts, though unevenly. Its spine is the
pairing of student \textit{projects} with academic \textit{papers}, the two we can
line up most directly. The physical \textit{parts} that teams register,
standardised fragments of DNA, give a text-independent check on whether the story
the text tells holds up. \textit{Patents}, the bridge from research to commercial
application and one of the P's the project is named for, are set up here but left
largely to future work, for practical reasons the Conclusion makes concrete.
Table~\ref{tab:artifacts} summarises what each artifact is and the role it plays.
A reader should leave this section knowing which promises the Results pay off, and
which are still roadmap.

% --- The ``Planet'' lens ------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The ``Planet'' lens: carbon capture}

The modern industrial era reshaped the planet. We burned through vast reserves of
ancient carbon, and in doing so we lived longer, fed more people, and grew past
every earlier limit. We also changed the climate. The change is large enough that
scientists have proposed a new geological epoch to mark it, the Anthropocene
\citep{crutzen2006anthropocene}, an age in which human activity is a dominant
force on the Earth system. We are terraforming our own planet, mostly by accident.

There is a hopeful reading of that same fact. If we can knock a planet's climate
off balance without trying, then the same power, aimed on purpose, might help set
it right. Biology is one of the best tools for the job, and carbon capture is
where this thesis watches it work. Humanity's oldest biotechnology is control over
fermentation: we brewed and baked with microbes long before we could name one.
Synthetic Biology turns that old craft to a new end, engineering microbes such as
\textit{E.\,coli} to pull carbon from industrial exhaust and build it into fuels
and materials \citep{delisiRoleSyntheticBiology2020, gleizerConversionEscherichiaColi2019}.

Carbon capture runs through the whole project as a single thread. It's concrete,
and we can trace it from a student's bench to a patent filing. We tag projects,
papers, and parts for their relevance to it, and follow the theme across all of
them. Late in the analysis it does a second job. Every artifact we study is
already synthetic biology, so any two of them look somewhat alike. Narrowing to
one sub-topic strips that shared baseline away, so we can ask whether local
relatedness still holds inside it.

% --- Unit of analysis --------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Why cities?}

Innovation in synthetic biology is not spread evenly across the map. It clusters,
and it clusters in cities. The reasons pile up in the same places: universities
with expensive equipment and talented students, venture capital for startups,
established industries like pharma that already own the infrastructure, and
regulators willing to permit the work. Deep-tech research needs all of these at
once, and cities are where they coincide.

Cities also specialise. Regions build capability in particular technologies, then
branch into adjacent ones over time \citep{hidalgoProductSpaceConditions2007}, so
different cities should develop different strengths \emph{within} synthetic
biology. A city with a strong software sector may build better computational
tools. One with deep agricultural roots may scale engineered crops more easily.
Where a research university dominates, the local edge may be foundational science
instead. This is the structure the thesis is after, and the reason the city is our
unit.

To read a city's strengths we pool its documents instead of judging them one at a
time. A single project or paper is a noisy signal, shaped as much by one team's
quirks as by the place around it. Pooled together, a city's output settles into
something steadier: a coarse-grained picture of what that place works on. We
aggregate across years as well, treating each city as one accumulated body of
work, since most cities produce too little in any single year to characterise on
their own. What we compare, in the end, is one city's body of work against
another's.

% --- Worked example ----------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{A worked example}

The case study is where this stops being abstract. Near the end we pick one
carbon-capture project and follow its threads outward: the BioBricks it
registered, the papers those parts were built from, the later papers that cite
them, and the patents that carry the same sequences. One project, traced through
every artifact type at once, shows in miniature the local trajectory the rest of
the thesis can only measure in aggregate.

% --- Scope and contributions -------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Scope and contributions}

A caution belongs here, at the front. This thesis shows relatedness. It does not
show causation. When a city's projects and papers sit close in meaning, many
shared causes could put them there: the same university, the same funding, the
same handful of advisors who mentor students by day and publish by night. We
cannot separate a real flow of ideas from a lab that simply houses both kinds of
work, and we do not try to. Every result that follows is a statement about
association and co-location, and we say so plainly wherever it matters.

The thesis makes four contributions, all concrete. The first is a corpus that puts
iGEM projects, academic papers, and BioBrick parts under one shared schema, each
geocoded to a city. The second is an embedding-based measure of how related a
city's student and academic work are. To keep that measure honest, the third is a
battery of permutation and placebo tests that a positive result has to survive.
The last is the pipeline itself, released as reproducible code and a public
website, so anyone can rerun the analysis or aim it at a different subfield.

% --- What to expect ----------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{A preview of the answer}

A brief word on where this lands, so the shape of the answer is clear before the
machinery arrives. Measured the obvious way, by the average position of a city's
work, projects and papers look almost identical everywhere. That similarity turns
out to be mostly the field talking: every document here is synthetic biology, so
every city starts out looking alike, and a permutation test strips the effect
away. The signal survives at a finer grain. When we ask whether a city's projects
and papers fall into the same specific topics, the answer is yes, well beyond
chance, and it holds up against the physical parts those teams built. The answer
to the question is a qualified yes, and earning that qualification is most of the
work.

% ============================================================
\section{Background}
% ============================================================

This thesis sits where three literatures meet. Its question, whether a city's
student and academic work are related, comes from the economic geography of
innovation and its principle of relatedness. Its method, comparing documents by
meaning, comes from natural language processing and the embedding models built for
scientific text. Its data, iGEM projects and the parts they register, comes from a
young science-of-science literature that has only lately taken student work
seriously. This section takes each in turn, and marks where this study departs from
them.

% --- Measuring the field -----------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Measuring a moving field}

Synthetic biology is hard to measure because it is hard to bound. It shares its
vocabulary, and often its journals, with the descriptive molecular biology it grew
out of, so a word count cannot tell the two apart. A molecular biologist might
study metabolic pathways in \textit{E.\,coli} with no interest in engineering
them. A synthetic biologist might describe the same pathway in nearly the same
words, meaning to rebuild it. \citet{oldhamSyntheticBiologyMapping2018} map the
field's patent landscape and hit exactly this problem of delimitation. Their
corpus is where we start.

The boundary also moves. Names for the same idea come and go as the field matures,
so a keyword list drawn up today mislabels the work of five years ago and misses
the work of five years from now. This is why building a corpus in a young field is
a running problem, revisited as the vocabulary shifts, and why the choices about
seed terms and citation expansion deserve the space this thesis gives them.

% --- Economic geography ------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The economic geography of relatedness}

Start with the geography. Innovation concentrates in space, and it has done so for
as long as anyone has measured it. Firms in the same industry gather in the same
regions to share labour, suppliers, and the loose talk that carries ideas from one
bench to the next. Economists call these agglomeration economies, and they matter
most in the knowledge-heavy work synthetic biology depends on. A city is more than
where the work happens. It is part of why the work happens.

Places do not diversify at random. A region is far likelier to move into an
activity that draws on what it already does than into one that starts from nothing.
This is the principle of relatedness: capabilities beget nearby capabilities, and
regional economies branch through the space of what is possible, each new activity
a short step from the last.

\citet{hidalgoProductSpaceConditions2007} made this measurable with the product
space. They could not observe a country's capabilities directly, so they inferred
relatedness from behaviour: two products count as related if the same countries
tend to export both. The resulting network predicts how economies grow and which
products a country is likely to add next. Relatedness, in this tradition, is
measured from what actually co-occurs.

The same logic runs through other proxies. Where products are related by the
countries that export both, industries can be related by the workers who move
between them: if people flow easily from one industry to another, the two must
draw on similar skills \citep{liEvaluatingPrincipleRelatedness2023}. Software work
has been mapped the same way, through the tasks and languages that careers pass
through \citep{fengBuildingBlocksSoftware}. Each proxy trades a different
observable behaviour for the same thing underneath, the capability itself.

% --- Relatedness in text -----------------------------------------------------
\subsection{From products to text}

This thesis measures relatedness a different way. Trade data and labour flows
reveal what a place \textit{does}; they say nothing about what its work is
\textit{about}. For that we turn to the text itself. Every artifact we study, a
project, a paper, a patent, carries a title and an abstract written in the
language of the field, and modern language models can place two such documents
near each other when they mean similar things. Relatedness measured from meaning
is the move this thesis makes, and it lets one method compare artifacts that share
no market and cite each other rarely.

\citet{boschmaScientificKnowledgeDynamics2014} show the approach can work.
Studying biotechnology across cities, they measure how scientific relatedness
shapes where new knowledge grows, and they work at the city level this thesis also
adopts. Theirs is the closest precedent for what follows: represent a place by
what it works on, and read relatedness off how those representations line up. Where
they use publications alone, we add the student projects and the physical parts.

One idea from this literature guides how we read the results: innovation is
path-dependent. What a place can do next is shaped by what it did before, so a
city's capabilities trace a trajectory through time, branching from year to year,
each step close to the one before. When this thesis speaks of a local innovation
trajectory, it means just this: a city's projects, papers, and parts moving
together through the space of the field, related because they grow from a shared
root. Whether that trajectory runs in a direction in time, with students leading
and papers following, is a question we test and cannot settle.

% --- iGEM as data ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{iGEM as a data source}

iGEM enters this thesis as data. Each team leaves behind a project wiki, an
informal, self-published account of a year's work, written by students at the
start of their research lives. That informality is a feature. The wikis are
interdisciplinary and candid in ways polished papers rarely are, and they capture
work that never reaches a journal. For a study of where synthetic biology is
taking root, they are a rare window onto the field's newest entrants, and they
have barely been used.

\citet{santoliniIGEMModelSystem2023} were among the first to treat this seriously,
presenting the iGEM record as a structured dataset for studying how teams
innovate. Their interest is the team: who joins, and what makes a group
productive. Ours is the place. Team dynamics sit outside this thesis, though they
plainly matter, and we ask instead whether a city's iGEM work lines up with the
research around it. Santolini's work establishes that the data can bear this kind
of weight.

What makes the data usable is iGEM's culture of openness. Teams are expected to
document everything in public and to deposit the genetic parts they use or build
into a shared registry, in a standard format meant to be reused. This norm, more
than any central archive, is why the record is rich enough to study: thousands of
comparable projects, each tied to a place and a year, each linked to the parts it
touched. The openness that defines iGEM as a community is also what makes it
legible as a dataset.

% --- BioBrick parts ----------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{BioBrick parts as a knowledge graph}

The parts follow a standard. A BioBrick is a fragment of DNA packaged so that any
two fragments join the same way, a convention introduced by Tom Knight at MIT so
that genetic parts could snap together like LEGO. Parts come in two kinds. A basic
part is a single piece of genetic code, often lifted straight from a published
result and translated into the format. A composite part is built from basic ones,
wired together into something that does more. Each part is meant to be reused and
recombined by teams that had no hand in making it.

Together the parts form a graph. A basic part points back to the paper it came
from. A composite part points to the basic parts inside it. A project points to
every part it used. Follow these links and the registry becomes a network that
ties projects to one another, and through the sourced parts, to the academic
literature. This structure lets a single iGEM project be read as a bundle of parts
that cite papers and other projects, and it is what lets the parts serve as
evidence in what follows.

The parts have one more use, and it is why they earn a place beside the text. A
team's parts are a record of what it actually built, kept entirely apart from the
words on its wiki. The mix of part types a city registers, how many promoters
against reporters against coding sequences, is a physical fingerprint of the kind
of biology it does. Because it owes nothing to the embedding model, it offers an
independent check: if the text-based picture of a city is real, the parts should
tell the same story. This thesis uses them for exactly that.

% --- Building the corpus -----------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Building the corpus}

Two strategies exist for gathering the papers, and each fails in its own
direction. A keyword search is precise but narrow: it finds documents that use the
field's terms and misses the foundational work those terms were built on. Citation
expansion is broad but leaky: it follows references outward from a seed set and
drags in neighbouring fields along the way. Coverage and precision trade off, and
no setting buys both. This thesis uses keywords for a defensible core and citation
expansion to reach the methods papers a keyword list would never name, and it
keeps the two layers labelled so the reader can see where each document came from.

% --- Shared semantic space ---------------------------------------------------
\subsection{A shared semantic space}

The artifacts speak different dialects. A patent is written to survive a lawyer, a
paper to persuade a reviewer, a wiki to explain a year's work to whoever visits.
To compare them we need a common representation that ignores the register and
keeps the meaning. A document embedding does this. It turns each title and
abstract into a point in a high-dimensional space, positioned so that documents
about similar things land near each other, whatever words they happen to use.

We build these points with SPECTER2, a language model from the Allen Institute
trained on scientific papers and their citations
\citep{cohanDocumentlevelRepresentation2020}. Its training objective is the one
that matters here: it learns to place two papers close together when one is likely
to cite the other. Relatedness is exactly what we are trying to measure, so a
model taught to predict citations is taught to do most of our work. SPECTER2
belongs to the BERT family of language models
\citep{devlinBERTPretrainingDeep2019}, but its scientific training is what sets it
apart from a general-purpose one.

Putting different artifact types in one embedding space is not a stretch we
invented. Recent work embeds papers and patents together to measure how research
turns into invention, adapting the same scientific-text models to the patent
register (Pat-SPECTER and PatentSBERTa are two examples). We lean on that
precedent when we place projects, papers, and parts side by side, and we inherit
its central assumption: that the artifacts are close enough in language for their
embeddings to be compared at all. Where that assumption strains, we say so.

% --- The gap -----------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The gap this fills}

Here is the gap this fills. Economic geography has mapped relatedness between
products, industries, and scientific fields, and left student projects untouched.
iGEM has been studied as a school for teams, rarely as a signal of where a city's
science is heading. No one has placed projects, papers, and parts in one semantic
space to ask whether a city's student and academic work occupy the same corners of
it. That question is the contribution.

The pieces are now on the table. From economic geography, a place is what it works
on, and relatedness is read off how those representations line up. From language
modelling, we can build those representations from text alone. From iGEM, we have
a novel artifact and a shared registry of parts to check it against. The next
chapter assembles these into a corpus, and the one after that into a measure.

% ============================================================
\section{Data and corpus construction}
% ============================================================

Before anything can be compared, it has to be made comparable. Projects, papers,
and parts arrive in different formats from different sources, so the first job is
to force them into one shape. Every artifact in this thesis carries the same
handful of fields: an identifier, a type, a title, a block of abstract-like text,
a year, and a place. Once the artifacts share a schema, the differences that
remain between them are differences of content, which is what we want to measure.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{A shared schema}

The schema is deliberately small. Text is the part that matters, so each artifact
contributes a title and an abstract-like passage: a paper's abstract, a project's
wiki, a patent's summary. Alongside the text sit the fields we need to place and
date each document, a year and a city, with country and coordinates carried along
for mapping. A few extra fields tag the carbon-capture case that later chapters
lean on. Anything a single source offers that the others cannot is dropped, so no
measure can secretly depend on it.

The schema lives in code, in a single module every ingest script imports, so a
field means the same thing whether it came from OpenAlex or the iGEM registry.
This is dull discipline, and it is what makes the pipeline reproducible: one
definition of a record, one place to change it, and no room for a stray column to
drift in from one source and not another.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Papers}

The papers come from OpenAlex, a free index of the world's scholarship that
publishes its metadata openly and without a paywall. We keep each paper's title
and abstract as its text, its publication year, and the institution of its first
author, which we later turn into a city. Openness is the reason for the choice: a
closed database might index more, but it could not be redistributed with the rest
of this project, and reproducibility is worth more here than a few percent of
coverage.

Finding the synthetic-biology papers is the hard part, for the reason the
Background gave: the field has no clean keyword boundary. We retrieve in three
layers, each covering the last one's blind spot. The first casts a narrow,
high-precision net. The second widens it to named subfields. The third follows
citations out of the core to catch what no keyword would.

The first layer is a short list of core terms, the phrases a paper can hardly
avoid if it is really about the field: \textit{synthetic biology} itself, along
with \textit{synthetic genomics} and a few close cousins. These queries are
precise. Almost everything they return belongs, but they return only the papers
that name the field outright, and miss the foundational work written before the
name settled.

The second layer adds the vocabulary of specific subfields, terms like
\textit{BioBrick}, \textit{repressilator}, and \textit{minimal genome} that mark
synthetic-biology work without using the field's name. These catch the applied and
technical papers the core terms miss, at some cost in precision, since a few
belong to neighbouring fields.

The third layer leaves keywords behind. Starting from the core set, we follow
citations in both directions, gathering the papers those core papers cite and the
papers that cite them. Seminal methods often carry none of the field's vocabulary
in their titles, and this is the only layer that reaches them, because influence,
not wording, is what pulls them in.

Citation expansion carries an obvious risk, and it is worth naming. Pull in enough
neighbours and you can inflate almost any pattern, so an expansion aimed at the
result would be a kind of quiet p-hacking. Ours is not. The seed set is fixed by
the core keywords before any analysis, the expansion follows citations
mechanically, and the layer each paper entered by is recorded, so a sceptical
reader can drop the expanded papers and check what survives.

After the three layers and de-duplication, the corpus holds \statNPapersTotal{}
papers spanning \statPaperYearMin{}--\statPaperYearMax{}. Papers before 2000 were
dropped: coverage that far back is thin and uneven, and the earliest iGEM projects
are a decade newer still, so old papers add noise to a comparison they can never
take part in.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{iGEM projects}

The projects come from iGEM's own registry, through its public team API. A first
pass pulls every team's identifier, name, institution, and competition year; a
second visits each team's wiki and lifts the project description into the text
field. Teams with no usable wiki, no title, or no description are dropped, since a
document with no text cannot be embedded.

This yields \statNProjectsTotal{} projects spanning
\statProjectYearMin{}--\statProjectYearMax{}. The record effectively begins in
2009, the point at which iGEM's documentation became consistent enough to scrape
at scale; before that, wikis are patchy and their formats vary too much to trust.

Each project's wiki is treated exactly like a paper's abstract: one block of text,
embedded the same way, compared on the same footing. We also collect each team's
roster where it is listed, a by-product we do not use in the analysis here but
leave in the corpus for the author-matching work the Conclusion sketches.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{BioBrick parts}

Every registered part was downloaded from the registry API, roughly 89{,}000
BioBricks in all. Parts are the one artifact with no text worth embedding; a part
is a sequence and a short functional label, not a document. We keep them for what
they are: a physical record of what each team built.

The registry sorts parts by function, and that taxonomy is what we use. A part is
a coding sequence, a promoter or other regulatory element, a ribosome binding
site, a terminator, a reporter, a composite device, and so on. Each label says
what job the part does in a genetic circuit, and the mix of labels a city
registers is the fingerprint the Background promised.

Where the Background described these links in principle, here is the number that
makes them usable: a little over half of all parts name a source publication, the
paper the sequence was taken from. That single field is the bridge between the
parts and the literature. We store it as an explicit set of link tables joining
parts to papers, composite parts to their components, and teams to the parts they
registered.

The last link matters most for geography. A part has no city of its own, but every
part was registered by a team, and every team, once geocoded, has one. So a part
inherits its team's city, and a project can be read as the bundle of parts it
registered, sitting in a place.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Geocoding}

Placing each artifact in a city is the hardest step in the whole pipeline, and the
one most likely to introduce error. Institutions hide behind acronyms, share names
across countries, move, merge, and rename. A team called \textit{iGEM Munich} is
easy; a team named for an obscure school abbreviation, in a language none of us
reads, is not.

Our first attempt used Nominatim, OpenStreetMap's free geocoder, on the raw
institution names. It failed more often than it worked. Many names matched
nothing, and some matched the wrong place confidently, which is worse. So
Nominatim moved to the end of the pipeline, a last resort instead of a first pass.

What worked was matching against structured institution registries. OpenAlex's
institutions API covers more than a hundred thousand organisations with clean
geographic data, and ROR adds the smaller players it misses, the high schools and
community labs where iGEM teams often sit. An exact match here is trustworthy in a
way a fuzzy text search never is.

For the teams that no registry resolved, we brought in language models. A first,
cheap pass with a small local model extracted a plausible city from each team's
name, country, and institution; the hard remainder went to a stronger model,
Claude Haiku. Every answer was cached, so the expensive calls run once and the
pipeline stays cheap to re-run.

Because a language model can invent a confident wrong answer, we did not take its
word on faith. We ran the same hard cases through several models and compared them
against the registry matches we trusted, keeping the approach only where the
models agreed with the ground truth often enough to rely on.

One limit is baked in and worth stating early. We geocode each artifact to a
single place, the first affiliation listed, so a genuinely multi-city
collaboration is flattened to one dot. The Munich team, which joins students from
two universities, becomes simply Munich. For a study that pools to the city this
is a real but bounded cost, and we return to it in the limitations.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Carbon-capture tagging}

The carbon-capture case study needs its own label, and we apply it by a documented
rule so it can be checked. Each project and paper is tagged for relevance to
microbial carbon capture, with a confidence score and a recorded reason attached.
The slice is therefore traceable: anyone can see why a given document was included
and drop the borderline ones. The result is a case study one can audit down to the
document.

The tagging flags 294 papers and 141 projects as carbon-capture work, spread
across a handful of cities. That is a small slice, and its size sets hard limits on
what the case study can claim, a point we keep in view when we get there. It cannot
carry statistical weight. Its value is focus: a single, legible corner of the field
in which to watch the method work.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Normalisation and the final corpus}

A last, unglamorous step makes the joins work. City names arrive messy,
capitalised and spelled inconsistently and padded with stray whitespace, so before
anything is grouped by city we strip and lowercase every name to a common key.
Without it, \textit{Cambridge} and \textit{cambridge} would count as two different
cities, and half the point of pooling would quietly break.

What comes out the other end is one corpus with three kinds of artifact, a shared
schema, a city on every record, and a web of links tying projects to parts and
parts to papers. A city enters the analysis only once it has both papers and
projects, since the whole question is how the two relate; \statNCitiesAnalyzed{}
cities clear that bar. Figure~\ref{fig:activity} shows the two corpora growing over
time: papers accumulate across the whole period, while projects appear only from
2009, and that offset shapes every temporal comparison that follows.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{activity_by_year}
  \caption{Yearly volume of papers (left) and iGEM projects (right). The two
  corpora cover overlapping but not identical periods, which constrains the
  temporal analysis in the Methods and Results.}
  \label{fig:activity}
\end{figure}

% ============================================================
\section{Methods}
% ============================================================

With the corpus in hand, the Methods turn text into numbers and numbers into
tests. Two pieces remain: a way to turn each document into something a computer can
compare, and a set of measures that capture relatedness without overstating it. We
build them in order, and show what each produces. Throughout we speak of
\textit{semantic relatedness} and \textit{association}, never cause, because the
artifacts we compare share so many local roots that no measure here could separate
a genuine flow of ideas from a university that simply houses both kinds of work.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Semantic embeddings}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

To compare text with numbers, we turn each document into a point in a shared
space. This is a \textit{semantic embedding space}, a high-dimensional space where
every document becomes a point and documents about similar things sit near each
other. Distance in that space is the thing we measure.

We generate the points with SPECTER2, the scientific-text model introduced in the
Background, run with its ``proximity'' adapter.\footnote{Model and adapter:
\url{https://huggingface.co/allenai/specter2}.} Each document goes in as its title
and abstract joined together, and comes back as a vector of 768 numbers. Because
SPECTER2 was trained to predict citations, documents it places close together are
documents likely to cite one another, which is exactly the relatedness we are
after.

Why embeddings, and not the obvious alternatives? Keyword counting is fragile
here: synthetic biology shares its vocabulary with descriptive molecular biology
\citep{oldhamSyntheticBiologyMapping2018}, so two documents can share words without
sharing meaning, or mean the same thing in different words. Citations barely exist
for student projects. Embeddings sidestep both problems, because they work from
meaning and not from surface form.

SPECTER2 returns unit-length vectors, so the natural measure of relatedness between
two documents is the cosine of the angle between them. Two documents pointing the
same way are closely related; two at right angles have nothing in common. This
cosine similarity is the building block for every measure below.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Representing cities as centroids}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

A city is not one document but a cloud of them. To compare cities we summarise
each cloud by its \textbf{centroid}, the average of all its document vectors,
rescaled to unit length. Each city gets two centroids, one for its papers and one
for its projects, each a coarse ``centre of mass'' of that kind of work in
semantic space.

A city's \textbf{semantic overlap} is the cosine similarity between its paper
centroid and its project centroid. Averaging first and comparing afterwards is a
standard shortcut: for unit-length vectors, the cosine of the two centroids equals
the average cosine over every paper--project pair, so we lose nothing by
summarising first (Turney \& Pantel, 2010). Representing a place by where its work
sits, and reading relatedness off how those positions line up, follows a long line
of work on regional capabilities and the product space
\citep{hidalgoProductSpaceConditions2007, boschmaScientificKnowledgeDynamics2014}.

Figure~\ref{fig:overlap} shows how the measure is distributed across the
\statNCitiesAnalyzed{} cities. Overlap is high and left-skewed, mean
\statOverlapMean{} and median \statOverlapMedian{}: most cities sit very close to
1.0, with a thin tail pulling the average down. The QQ plot confirms the departure
from normality (skewness \statOverlapSkew{}), which matters for any later model
that assumes well-behaved errors. Table~\ref{tab:summary} gives the full summary
statistics, and Table~\ref{tab:top15} lists the highest-overlap cities. They are
the large, established hubs with long iGEM histories, which is reassuring but, as
the next paragraph shows, also a warning.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{overlap_distribution}
  \caption{Distribution of city-level semantic overlap (left) and a QQ plot
  against the normal distribution (right). Overlap clusters near 1.0 because all
  documents belong to the same broad field; the spread that remains is what the
  rest of the analysis tries to explain.}
  \label{fig:overlap}
\end{figure}

\input{generated/tables/summary_stats.tex}

\input{generated/tables/top15_cities.tex}

That high baseline is a warning. Every document in the corpus is synthetic
biology, so any two city centroids start out close just by belonging to the same
field. Larger cities make it worse: with more documents averaged into each
centroid, their centres are steadier and land nearer the field-wide average.
Figure~\ref{fig:size} shows the effect plainly. Overlap rises with the number of
papers ($r = \statSizePapersR{}$) and projects ($r = \statSizeProjectsR{}$) a city
has. This is the old tension between diversity and relatedness in regional
science, and it means raw overlap cannot stand on its own as evidence of local
idea flow. The measures that follow are built to see past this baseline.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{overlap_vs_size}
  \caption{Semantic overlap against city size, measured by paper count (left)
  and project count (right) on a log scale. Both relationships are strongly
  positive, so part of a city's overlap reflects how much it produces rather
  than how aligned its two outputs are.}
  \label{fig:size}
\end{figure}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Beyond centroids: do projects and papers share the same topics?}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

The centroid measure has the ceiling we just saw: every document is synthetic
biology, so two city centroids start close by default, and the spread that
survives is thin and tangled up with city size. A sharper question sidesteps the
average. Instead of measuring how nearly two centroids point the same way, we ask
\textit{which specific topics} a city works on, and whether its students and its
scholars work on the \textit{same} ones.

To do that we first sort the documents into topics. The 768-dimensional embeddings
are too sparse to cluster directly, a symptom of the curse of dimensionality, so we
compress them to a few dozen dimensions with UMAP, which keeps the local
neighbourhoods that matter here (McInnes, Healy \& Melville, 2018). Over that
reduced space we run HDBSCAN, a density-based algorithm that finds clusters without
being told how many to look for and sets the sparse leftovers aside as noise
(Campello, Moulavi \& Sander, 2013). The result is a few hundred coherent
sub-themes, things like biosensors, metabolic engineering, and genome assembly. We
label each one by passing its most central titles through a language model, which
gives the clusters names a reader can recognise.

Each city then gets two \textit{cluster-frequency vectors}: the share of its papers
in each topic, and the share of its projects. A city's \textbf{cluster
co-membership} is the cosine between those two vectors. Unlike the centroid
overlap, it scores high \textit{only} when papers and projects sit in the same
specific topics, and near zero when they do not. The field-level baseline cancels
out, because belonging to synthetic biology is no longer enough to score.

That sharpness costs data. With several hundred topics, a city holding only a
handful of documents can miss its own themes by chance, so its two vectors look
unrelated for lack of observations, not lack of relatedness. We therefore compute
the measure only for cities with at least \statClusterMinDocs{} clustered documents
of each type, which leaves \statClusterNCitiesDense{} of the
\statClusterNCitiesAll{} cities that have clustered work of both kinds. A sweep
across thresholds shows this is a measurement floor, not a finding: below it most
cities score exactly zero, and above it a signal appears and strengthens as the
threshold rises.

We then put the measure through the test the centroid overlap could not pass, a
\textbf{re-pairing permutation test}. Within each country we randomly reassign
which city's project vector is matched against which city's paper vector, recompute
the average co-membership, and repeat two thousand times (Good, 2005). Shuffling
within countries keeps each country's mix of work intact while breaking the local
pairing, so the test isolates the one thing we care about: whether a city's own two
outputs align more than a same-country neighbour's would.

The result clears the bar. The observed mean co-membership is
\statClusterPermObserved{}, against a null mean of \statClusterPermNullMean{}
(permutation $p = \statClusterPermP{}$), an excess of \statClusterPermExcess{},
about half again above chance. And it is not a size effect: regressed on the log
counts of a city's papers and projects, it leaves only $R^2 = \statClusterOlsRsq{}$,
with neither coefficient significant ($p = \statClusterSizePapersP{}$ and
$\statClusterSizeProjectsP{}$). Figure~\ref{fig:cluster} sets the centroid measure
and the permutation null side by side.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{cluster_comembership}
  \caption{Cluster co-membership. Left: the distribution of the centroid overlap
  (pinned near 1.0 by the shared field) against cluster co-membership, which spreads
  out because it scores only shared \textit{specific} topics. Right: the
  within-country re-pairing permutation null for the mean co-membership across cities
  with at least \statClusterMinDocs{} documents of each type; the observed value sits
  far into the right tail ($p = \statClusterPermP{}$), passing the test the centroid
  measure fails.}
  \label{fig:cluster}
\end{figure}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Local alignment: is a project closer to its own city?}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

We can also work one project at a time. Is an individual iGEM project more like its
\textit{own} city's papers than the papers of every other city? If projects and
papers share local roots, the answer should be yes.

For each project we compute its cosine similarity to its home city's paper
centroid, and its average similarity to the paper centroids of all other cities
(keeping only cities with at least three papers, so the centroids are stable).
The difference between the two, which we call $\delta$, is positive whenever a
project looks more like home than like elsewhere. Across \statAlignNProjects{}
projects the mean advantage is $\delta = \statAlignMeanDelta{}$, and
\statAlignFracPos{} of projects are individually positive.
Figure~\ref{fig:align} shows the full distribution and the project-by-project
comparison.

A word on counting, because it changes the headline. Projects from the same city
are all compared against the \textit{same} paper centroid, so they are not
independent. A naive one-sample test ($t = \statAlignT{}$) badly overstates its
confidence, treating \statAlignNProjects{} correlated projects as that many
independent draws. The honest unit is the city. Clustering the standard error at
the city level (the intercept-only case of the cluster-robust estimator of Cameron
\& Miller, 2015) brings the statistic down to $t = \statAlignTClustered{}$ across
\statAlignNCities{} cities. Aggregating to one mean $\delta$ per city before testing
tells the same story ($\delta = \statAlignDeltaCity{}$, $t = \statAlignTCity{}$,
with \statAlignFracCitiesPos{} of cities on the home-city side).

The effect is small in absolute terms, a consequence of the field-level baseline,
but it is real and it survives being counted properly. We read it as local
\textit{relatedness}, not a causal pull: a shared university faculty could produce
both kinds of work on the same theme without one feeding the other.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{project_level_alignment}
  \caption{Local alignment at the project level. Left: the distribution of
  $\delta$, each project's similarity to its own city's papers minus its mean
  similarity to other cities' papers; mass to the right of zero indicates local
  alignment. Right: own-city versus other-city similarity, where points above
  the diagonal are the locally aligned projects.}
  \label{fig:align}
\end{figure}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Stable specialisation versus local timing: a difference-in-differences design}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

The local advantage could mean two very different things. It might be a genuine,
time-specific connection: this year's projects tracking this year's local papers.
Or it might be a city's stable identity, a place that has always worked on
biosensors having both projects and papers about biosensors every year, with no
idea passing between them. To tell these apart we borrow the logic of a
\textbf{difference-in-differences} design, the workhorse of applied econometrics
(Angrist \& Pischke, 2009).

The idea is a two-by-two comparison. For each project we measure its similarity
to its own city's papers and to other cities' papers, and we do this both in the
project's \textit{own year} and in \textit{other years}. A stable-specialisation
story predicts a home-city advantage even in other years; a local-timing story
predicts an \textit{extra} advantage in the project's own year, on top of that.
The difference-in-differences is exactly that extra slice. Table~\ref{tab:did}
reports the four cells, and Figure~\ref{fig:did} shows them alongside the
distribution of the per-project estimate.

\input{generated/tables/did_cells.tex}

Across \statDidN{} projects the estimate is positive and survives the same
city-level clustering used above ($\text{DiD} = \statDidEstimate{}$,
$t = \statDidTClustered{}$ clustered across \statDidNCities{} cities; the naive
$t = \statDidT{}$ again overstates the precision), but it is tiny next to the
stable-specialisation gap that sits underneath it. In plain terms: most of why a
project resembles its city's papers is that the city has a durable thematic
identity, with only a sliver attributable to same-year alignment. This is a
useful corrective to a naive reading of the local-alignment result, and we return
to it as the analytical centrepiece of the Results.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{did_alignment}
  \caption{Difference-in-differences. Left: mean similarity in each of the four
  city\,$\times$\,year cells. Right: the distribution of the per-project
  difference-in-differences; its small positive mean is the part of local
  alignment that is specific to the project's own year.}
  \label{fig:did}
\end{figure}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Temporal structure: do projects lead papers?}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

The guiding intuition of this thesis is that student projects might introduce
early ideas that academic papers later develop. If so, a city's projects in year
$t$ should look most like its papers a few years \textit{after} $t$. To test the
shape of this relationship we build annual centroids for each city's projects and
papers, and for every project-year we record its similarity to the city's paper
centroid at offsets from three years before to three years after. Averaging over
all city-years gives a \textbf{lead--lag profile}: similarity as a function of
the offset $k$, where positive $k$ means papers come after projects. This is the
descriptive, correlational cousin of a Granger lead--lag analysis (Granger,
1969); we use it to describe timing, not to claim causation.

Figure~\ref{fig:leadlag} and Table~\ref{tab:leadlag} show the result, and the
honest summary is that the profile is nearly flat. The nominal peak sits at
$k = \statLeadlagBestLag{}$ (mean similarity \statLeadlagBestSim{}), the direction
the early-signal idea predicts, but the whole range spans about a thousandth of a
cosine unit and the confidence intervals overlap almost everywhere. We read this as
a limit of resolution: city-level annual centroids, often built from a single
document in a year, are too coarse to show a lead--lag signal even if one exists.
We report the test because its failure says something about the method, not because
it settles the question.

\input{generated/tables/lead_lag.tex}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.72\linewidth]{lead_lag_profile}
  \caption{Lead--lag profile between project and paper centroids, with 95\%
  bootstrap confidence intervals. Positive lags mean papers follow projects. The
  profile is close to flat, so the data neither confirm nor rule out the
  early-signal hypothesis.}
  \label{fig:leadlag}
\end{figure}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Beyond text: BioBrick part-type composition}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

Everything so far rests on text. As an independent check, we turn to the physical
parts each city's teams registered. The \textit{mix} of part types a city deposits,
its coding sequences, regulatory elements, reporters, and so on, is a fingerprint
of the kind of biology it does, and it owes nothing to the embedding space. If the
text-based picture is capturing something real, the two should broadly agree.

For each city with at least ten registered parts (\statNCitiesParts{} cities in
all) we compute the share of its parts in each functional category, and summarise
how specialised that mix is with its Shannon entropy: low entropy means a city
concentrates on one type of part, high entropy means it spreads across many. The
median city sits at \statPartEntropyMedian{} nats, well below the
\statPartEntropyMax{} nats a perfectly even spread would give, so cities do tend
to specialise. Figure~\ref{fig:parts} shows the spread of specialisation and the
part-type fingerprints of the most active cities.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{part_type_composition}
  \caption{BioBrick part-type composition. Left: the distribution of part-type
  entropy across cities; most cities lean toward specialisation. Right: the
  part-type profile of the thirty cities with the most registered parts, sorted
  so that cities with a shared dominant type sit together.}
  \label{fig:parts}
\end{figure}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Interpretive caution}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

Two limits shape how far these measures can be pushed, and they belong here, not
buried later. The first is the field baseline. Because the whole corpus is
synthetic biology, cosine similarity between city centroids is dominated by
field-level similarity: two cities look alike mostly because both do synthetic
biology, and only secondarily because of any local alignment. The
difference-in-differences result makes this concrete, and it is why we lean on the
within-city comparisons over raw overlap. Even the sharpest of them, cluster
co-membership, carries a caveat: it needs enough documents to estimate a topic
distribution, so its permutation result speaks to the \statClusterNCitiesDense{}
most active cities, not the long tail.

The second limit is resolution. Each artifact is geocoded to a single affiliation,
so multi-city collaborations are flattened, and the annual centroids are too thin
for fine temporal claims. So we frame every result here as semantic relatedness and
plausible co-location, and leave claims of causal knowledge flow to future work
with finer, author- and mentor-level data.

% ============================================================
\section{Results}
% ============================================================

The Methods section reported each measure's numbers where it built the measure.
Here we step back and read those numbers as a sequence of escalating claims, each
more demanding than the last. The first is a sanity check: that the embedding space
recovers a recognisable map of the field at all. The second is the thesis's central
empirical claim: that a city's student projects and its academic papers occupy the
\textit{same specific topics}, not merely the same broad field --- a local
relatedness that, measured by cluster co-membership, survives a permutation test the
raw centroid overlap cannot. A project-level alignment test corroborates it from a
second direction, and decomposing that alignment shows how much is live, same-year
coupling (little) versus standing thematic identity (most). The third claim is the
most ambitious, and the one we can least support: that the two are linked in time,
with projects running ahead of papers. We take them in turn, then ask whether
anything outside the text agrees.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The Embedding Space Recovers a Sensible Map}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

Before asking whether projects and papers align, we should check that the space
they live in is meaningful. Two features suggest it is. The cities with the
highest project--paper overlap (Table~\ref{tab:top15}) are precisely the places
one would name without any model in hand: Cambridge, Boston and Berkeley in the
United States; Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin and Wuhan in China; Munich and Marburg
in Germany; Paris in France --- large, long-running synthetic biology hubs with
deep iGEM histories. The cities at the other end (Table~\ref{tab:bottom15}) are
almost all places with a single paper and a single project, where a centroid is
just one document and overlap is whatever that lone pairing happens to be. Low
overlap, in other words, tracks thin data rather than genuine thematic
divergence, exactly as the size relationship ($r = \statSizePapersR{}$ for
papers, $r = \statSizeProjectsR{}$ for projects) leads us to expect. The map
behaves the way a sensible map should: it puts the well-known hubs at the top and
reserves its uncertainty for the cities we know least about.

\input{generated/tables/bottom15_cities.tex}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{A City's Projects and Papers Share Its Specific Topics}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

The central finding is that a city's student projects and its academic papers
concentrate in the \textit{same specific corners} of synthetic biology, not just the
same broad field. Measured as cluster co-membership --- the cosine between a city's
paper and project topic-distributions --- the average city, among the
\statClusterNCitiesDense{} with enough documents to measure it, scores
\statClusterPermObserved{}, well above the \statClusterPermNullMean{} expected when
we re-pair papers and projects across same-country cities at random (permutation
$p = \statClusterPermP{}$). In plain terms: a city's two kinds of output land in the
same topics far more often than a comparable neighbour's would, and the gap is large
relative to chance --- an excess of \statClusterPermExcess{}, roughly half again
above the null.

What makes this the result the draft leans on, rather than the raw centroid overlap,
is that it clears two bars the centroid measure cannot. It is not an artifact of the
field baseline: by scoring only shared \textit{specific} topics, it starts from zero
for unrelated cities rather than from the near-1.0 floor every synthetic-biology
centroid sits on. And it is not an artifact of city size: the same kind of regression
that explains most of the centroid overlap explains almost none of this measure
($R^2 = \statClusterOlsRsq{}$, with neither size coefficient significant), so we are
not merely rediscovering that large cities have steadier centres. A measure built to
survive both objections does survive them, which is why we read its permutation
result as the thesis's strongest evidence of genuine local relatedness.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Projects and Papers Co-specialise Within Cities}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

A second line of evidence works one project at a time: an iGEM project sits closer
to its own city's papers than to other cities' papers. The raw advantage is small but pervasive ---
$\delta = \statAlignMeanDelta{}$, with \statAlignFracPos{} of projects on the
home-city side --- and, crucially, it holds up once we count cities rather than
projects. Clustered at the city level the advantage stands at
$t = \statAlignTClustered{}$ across \statAlignNCities{} cities, and
\statAlignFracCitiesPos{} of cities (not just projects) lean toward home.
Whatever else is true, a city's student work really does resemble its own
academic work more than a stranger's.

But ``closer to home'' can mean two very different things, and separating them is
the analytical heart of this draft. The home-city advantage might be a
\textit{timing} signal --- this year's projects tracking this year's local
papers, the kind of live coupling a knowledge pipeline would produce --- or it
might be pure \textit{stable specialisation}: a city that has always done
biosensors will show biosensor projects and biosensor papers in every year, with
no ideas passing between them. The difference-in-differences design isolates the
timing slice from the standing one (Table~\ref{tab:did}). The verdict is sobering
for the pipeline story: of the whole home-city advantage, only \statDidEstimate{}
is specific to a project's own year ($t = \statDidTClustered{}$ clustered across
\statDidNCities{} cities --- small, but really there), while the rest is a
durable thematic identity that holds across years. Co-specialisation is real, but
it is mostly something a city \textit{is}, not something that \textit{happens}
between its students and its scholars in a given year. This is a more modest claim
than a knowledge pipeline, and it is the one the data actually support.

That co-specialisation is also unevenly distributed, in a way that is itself
informative. The home-city advantage grows with the size of a city's research
base: across cities, mean $\delta$ rises with the (log) number of local papers
($r = \statAlignSizeR{}$), and projects in above-median cities enjoy more than
three times the advantage of those in the long tail ($\delta =
\statAlignDeltaLarge{}$ versus $\statAlignDeltaSmall{}$). Local alignment, in
other words, is largely a feature of mature clusters --- the Beijings and Bostons
with enough of both kinds of work to have built a coherent local identity --- and
fades, without quite vanishing, in cities with only a project or two. That is a
more useful finding for innovation policy than a flat average would be: it
suggests the project--paper link is something clusters \textit{grow into} as
their research base thickens.

Finally, the carbon-capture case study behaves just like the whole. Restricting
the alignment test to the \statCcAlignN{} carbon-capture projects (across
\statCcAlignNCities{} cities) gives essentially the same picture as the full
corpus --- $\delta = \statCcAlignMeanDelta{}$, \statCcAlignFracPos{} of projects
on the home-city side, $t = \statCcAlignTClustered{}$ clustered by city. The
thread we promised to follow is not an exception: a city's carbon-capture
students sit nearer its own carbon-relevant literature than elsewhere's, exactly
as the general result predicts.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Timing Is Unresolved, but the Parts Agree}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

The most ambitious claim --- that projects lead papers --- we cannot make, and the
reason is worth stating as a result in its own right. The lead--lag profile
(Table~\ref{tab:leadlag}, Figure~\ref{fig:leadlag}) rises gently from lag $-3$ to
lag $+3$, with its nominal peak at $k = \statLeadlagBestLag{}$ years, the
direction the early-signal hypothesis predicts. But the whole profile spans about
a thousandth of a cosine unit and the confidence intervals overlap throughout, so
we treat it as flat. This is best read as a \textit{negative methodological
result}: a centroid averaged over the one or two documents a small city produces
in a given year carries almost no temporal information, so timing simply cannot be
read off centroids at this resolution. Resolving it will take a sharper instrument
--- the project--part--paper citation graph described in the Background, where a
single project's parts point to dated literature directly --- which we flag as the
natural next step rather than a finding of this draft.

What does survive is an independent corroboration from outside the text. The mix
of BioBrick part types a city registers --- measured with no reference to the
embedding space --- shows the same specialisation the text does
(Figure~\ref{fig:parts}): the median city's part-type entropy is
\statPartEntropyMedian{} nats against a possible \statPartEntropyMax{}, so cities
concentrate on particular kinds of biology rather than spreading evenly. More
directly, cities that look alike in part-type space also look alike in
topic-cluster space: correlating the two sets of city-to-city similarities --- a
Mantel test (Mantel, 1967) --- gives a clear positive association across
\statMantelNCities{} cities ($r = \statMantelR{}$, $p = \statMantelP{}$ against a
label-shuffling null), so the physical parts and the abstract text rank the cities
the same way. That two methods built on entirely different data --- abstract text on
one side, registered parts on the other --- both point to local specialisation gives
us more confidence that the specialisation lives in the cities, not in the model.

% ============================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% ============================================================

The question this draft set out to answer was whether cities that host student
synthetic biology projects also produce academic papers in related areas. The
answer is a qualified yes. Its strongest form is topical: in cities active enough to
measure it, a city's projects and papers fall in the \textit{same specific}
sub-fields far more than a same-country neighbour's would (cluster co-membership,
permutation $p = \statClusterPermP{}$), a relatedness that holds up after stripping
out both the field-level baseline and city size. The centroid-based tests tell the
same story from a second angle. A city's iGEM projects sit measurably nearer its own
papers than other cities' papers; the pattern holds across roughly nine of every
ten projects and, more tellingly, across four in five \textit{cities} once the
inference is clustered where it belongs; it is strongest in large, mature research
hubs but still positive in the long tail; it reappears essentially unchanged in
the carbon-capture case study; and it is echoed by a parts-based fingerprint that
never touches the embedding model. Cities do appear to specialise, and their
student and academic work specialises together.

Two qualifications keep that finding honest. First, the alignment is mostly a
stable feature of a city's identity rather than a year-by-year coupling: the
difference-in-differences result shows that the same-year, ``this project tracks
this paper'' component, while statistically real even under city-level
clustering, is small next to the standing thematic gap. We therefore describe a
\textit{local innovation trajectory} as shared standing specialisation, not as a
demonstrated flow of ideas from students to scholars. Second, our strongest
temporal hypothesis --- that projects run ahead of papers --- is neither confirmed
nor refuted; the city--year centroids are too thin to resolve it, and resolving it
will take the finer, graph-level instrument we turn to below. Both qualifications
echo the interpretive caution in the Methods: with a corpus that is entirely
synthetic biology, field-level similarity sets a high baseline, and the signal we
care about lives in the small margins on top of it.

These limits also point the way forward, and mark where the project's remaining
reach --- patents, and the planet-scale application that motivates the whole
effort --- comes in. The clearest gains would come from finer links than centroids
can provide: scraping the DOIs that iGEM teams cite on their wikis, to build a
direct citation network between projects and the local literature; matching paper,
patent, and team authors to ask whether researchers stay in the orbit of their old
iGEM collaborators; and matching BioBrick sequences to patent filings through
sequence databases, to trace individual pieces of genetic code from an open
registry into commercial application. Each would replace a coarse, centroid-level
association with a concrete, traceable link --- and would let a future study ask
not just whether a city's projects and papers are related, but whether one
actually grew out of the other.
